name: Earthly Lunar
tagline: Instrumentation and observability for the software delivery pipeline: builds, tests, CI, and deploys in one place.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The uncomfortable thing about SDLC observability is that the data belongs to you already: GitHub, your CI provider, and your deploy tooling all expose it over API. An agent can absolutely build a personal dashboard that polls one CI system, stores runs and PRs in SQLite, and computes deploy frequency, lead time, build duration, and failure rates in a single sitting. What it cannot build in a sitting is broad instrumentation across every CI provider, test runner, and build tool that a real engineering org actually runs, plus the collector maintenance when those APIs shift. For one person watching one repo, the DIY version is honestly fine. For a team that wants trustworthy numbers across heterogeneous pipelines and nobody assigned to babysit the ingestion, the product is doing real work.
coreLoopDIY: Polls the GitHub API for workflow runs, pull requests, and deployments, stores them locally, and renders delivery metrics and build-time trends on a dashboard.
requirements: GitHub personal access token with repo and actions read scope
Node 20 and a machine or small VM to run the poller on a schedule
Repos you actually have read access to
whatYouLose: Coverage beyond one CI provider: other runners, local builds, and non-GitHub deploy paths go unmeasured
Test-level and step-level granularity, including flaky test attribution across runs
Cross-team rollups and any notion of a shared, agreed-upon metric definition
Someone else fixing the collectors when upstream APIs change shape
Alerting and anomaly detection, so regressions show up only when you open the tab
moatNotes: The integration surface is the product. Your own pipeline data is not proprietary to them, but stitching it together across every tool a team uses is the part nobody wants to own.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because delivery metrics are only useful when everyone trusts them, and trust comes from coverage plus consistency. A homegrown dashboard that reads one CI provider gets argued with the first time a number looks wrong, and then someone spends a sprint on ingestion bugs instead of the thing they were trying to fix. Paying makes the numbers somebody else's job, which for a team is usually cheaper than it looks on the invoice.
notes: The pipeline data is already yours; the pain is collecting it from six places forever.
prompt:
Build a local SDLC metrics dashboard for my own GitHub repos. Single project, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/metrics.db
- Recharts for charts
- No auth, no multi-tenancy, no Docker

Secrets in .env.local: GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_REPOS (comma separated owner/repo list).

Ingestion:
- A script at scripts/sync.ts run via "npm run sync", safe to re-run, idempotent upserts by id
- Pull per repo: workflow runs (with conclusion, timing, head_sha, branch), pull requests (created, merged, first commit time), deployments and deployment statuses
- Handle pagination and rate limit headers, back off on 403 secondary limits
- Store raw fields plus a normalized events table, keep a sync_state table with last cursor per repo and resource

Metrics page:
- Deploy frequency per week, computed from successful deployments or merges to the default branch if no deployments exist
- Lead time for change: first commit to merge, median and p90
- Change failure rate: share of default-branch workflow runs that failed
- Build duration trend per workflow, median and p90, plus the ten slowest runs
- Per-job failure counts and a simple flaky signal: same workflow and head_sha with both a failed and a passing attempt
- Filters for repo, branch, and a date range of 7, 30, or 90 days

Explicitly out of scope: non-GitHub CI providers, test result parsing from artifacts, Slack alerting, user management, hosted deployment.

Deliver: README with setup and the exact metric definitions used, npm scripts for dev and sync, and a seed script that inserts fake data so the UI renders before the first real sync.
